messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: more prior advice needed
parts:
I'm updating the manual for the 2.4 release and I'm
still short some advice I'd hoped to get on default priors.

First, what should we use for a scale parameter, say in
a simple linear regression, or elsewhere?

Second, the other hole in our generic prior advice is for
ordered and positive ordered vectors.

As far as I can tell from thinking and simulation,

parameters {
ordered[K] y;
}
model {
y ~ normal(0,1);
}

gives the same results for y as:

parameters {
vector[K] y_raw;
}
transformed parameters {
vector[K] y;
y <- sort(y_raw);
}
model {
y ~ normal(0,1);
}

So this makes sense if we're thinking of the ordered vector
as the result of K independent draws that are sorted.

But that doesn't quite seem right for logistic regression cutpoints.
Maybe for that, we'd want to put a prior on the differences?

for (k in 2:K)
(y[k] - y[k-1]) ~ ... something with support over positive values ...

Anyway, I'm just going to punt for now and hopefully get some
advice for going forward for 2.4.0++ (the next release after 2.4.0).

- Bob

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: What is a good default prior for a scale parameter?
parts:
What is a good default prior for a scale parameter? I think we can have different levels of defaults.

0. Noninformative priors

Simplest is just uniform on (0, infinity). That’s our default default and it seems fine to me, although it can have problems if the number of observations is small.

Another option is uniform on log(sigma) but this has the problem of failing for hierarchical models. This does reduce to the standard result for linear regression so in some sense we need to consider it for “backward compatibility” with conventional Bayesian inference, but really I feel that this prior is more trouble than it’s worth.

For point estimation with hierarchical models, we recommend gamma(2,1/A) for some large value of A (or, most simply, gamma(2,0)); this is discussed at exhausting length in our recent Psychometrika paper. This prior keeps the point estimate away from 0 which is a practical necessity in many applications of hierarchical models.

1. Weakly informative priors

If number of observations (or, in a hierarchical model, the number of groups) is small, then we’ll want to control the estimation of the scale parameter at the high end. One choice that I’ve recommended in the past (most notably, in my 2006 Bayesian Analysis paper) is half-Cauchy with peak at 0 and scale A, where A is some large value. A=10 would not be a bad choice, I think. Of course it’s easy to imagine a situation where the user would need a much larger scale (for example, in a model where the data have not been normalized), but in that case it is the user’s responsibility to set a larger value.

I could even imagine some sort of diagnostic, where if the posterior estimate of the scale parameter is comparable to or higher than the prior scale, that we issue a warning, something like: “Attention: estimate of parameter sigma_y is high compared to the prior distribution. Check the scale of your model and, if necessary, rescale your data or increase the upper scale of your prior distribution.”

For point estimation, we could go with gamma(2,1/A), with A set to some default value such as 10.

2. Informative priors

A lot depends on what sort of information is available. But one way to frame this is in terms of hierarchical models. Suppose we have a model with many scale parameters: sigma1, sigma2, sigma3, etc. By default we’ll want to give them a common prior with unknown hyperparameters. And then if more info is available it could be natural to set things up as a regression model on log(sigma) with predictors at the level of the variance component. This suggests a lognormal model: log(sigma_j) ~ normal(mu,tau), and then we need priors on mu and tau.

What sort of informative priors on mu, tau would be good here? I’m not sure, but the point is that we can also use this model when we have only one variance component, in which case we have a model that is set up as a mixture-of-lognormals. That said, once we’ve set it up we probably would want to avoid the mixture formulation as it could make the computation run slower.


OK, another question: what’s a good default prior for a covariance matrix? We have various uniform-like options, also for point estimation there’s the Wishart (_not_ inverse-Wishart) which we recommend in our forthcoming JEBS paper.

We're recommending scaling a correlation matrix with an lkj prior.

For point estimation with hierarchical models, we recommend gamma(2,1/A) for some large value of A (or, most simply, gamma(2,0)); this is discussed at exhausting length in our recent Psychometrika paper.  This prior keeps the point estimate away from 0 which is a practical necessity in many applications of hierarchical models.

No, Bugs etc. use _inverse_-Wisharts.  What I’m talking about here is plain old Wishart, which when given the appropriate scale parameter keeps the point estimate away from the non-positive-definite boundary, something that a uniform prior doesn’t do.  Again it’s the difference between a prior for point estimation vs a prior for rull Bayes.

>> then y[0] will be the first rank statistic for K normal(0,1)
>> draws.
>
> Yes, y[0] will be, but the _prior_ for the value of y[0] should not be
> normal(0,1) here. The *prior* for the value of y[0] should take the
> distribution of the first order statistic for K normal(0,1) draws, and
> that distribution is not normal. (For example it's clearly not
> symmetric around zero; a priori we expect it to be low.)

There are two models, which may be part of the confusion.

In the model with explicit sorting, the prior for y_raw is
normal(0,1), but the prior for y isn't i.i.d. normal, as
there is sorting involved.

In the ordered vector model, the prior is not i.i.d. because
of the sorting constraint.

In both cases you get a kind of dependence in the prior for y.
In the y_raw case, the y_raw values are generated i.i.d., but
then sorted to get what you want.

I'm not very good at all of this, relative to the other members
of the Stan dev team and many of our users, which is why I was
asking for help in the first place. So I may still be misunderstanding
something fundamental here myself. I certainly can't connect
why the two models give the same behavior theoretically.

- Bob

parts:
For a comparision of LKJ to (inverse) Wishart, see Ben's paper:

http://andrewgelman.com/2012/08/30/visualizing-distributions-of-covariance-matrices/

lkj(1) is equivalent to a uniform prior on correlation matrices.
In Stan, you get a uniform prior if you don't specify anything.
It's proper for correlation matrices because they're bounded.

Using Cholesky factors is usually more efficient, but I don't think
we have a Cholesky factor version of the Wisharts (or even if it's
possible).

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] What is a good default prior for a scale parameter?
parts:
On Tuesday, August 26, 2014 1:05:48 PM UTC-4, Mauricio Garnier-Villarreal wrote:
Is there any substantial benefit of the lkj over the wishart, or over a non-informative (uniform) correlation matrix? Or could they be equivalent?

For optimization, one could argue for setting eta > 1 as the shape parameter for the lkj_corr density so that singular correlation matrices have zero density as opposed to just zero measure. For MCMC, that shouldn't be a major concern so you can set eta = 1 and then comment it out of your Stan program because it implies a uniform density. Thus, if you use eta > 1, it is because you substantively want to concentrate the prior density more on the identity matrix.

However, if the parameter is a covariance matrix, then you would need to specify a distribution for the standard deviations as well. That could be a lot of things, but if you do it poorly, the whole model could suffer.

I don't think there is much to be said for Wishart or inverse Wishart. Traditionally, they are used in Gibbs samplers because they are conjugate with the multivariate normal. Conjugacy is irrelevant for Stan, but one thing that is relevant is that you can integrate the covariance matrix out of the prior

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse-Wishart_distribution#Conjugate_distribution

and integrating out nuisance parameters means less work for Stan.

Ben
